findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and why it matters. The next two paragraphs explain that this page is a study of another project. So the reader can tell the two products apart even though the title names both.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The first section after the navigation is an error message that repeats the job id. It sits before "Start here", so a newcomer's first look at evidence is a failure. It undercuts the opening promise that the page shows the models, verdict and cost behind each change.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This link is for the repository owner, not a first-time visitor, yet it appears in the header next to the newcomer's next step. A newcomer may be unsure whether it applies to them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: clone, install, then a one-line command to try, with a note on what it acts on and that it waits for Enter. But the list mentions cargo without listing Rust or cargo as a prerequisite, so a reader without Rust may not know whether setup.sh installs it.
findings.source: Next steps: "git 2.40 or later; a C linker (cc), which cargo needs to build Athena; curl...; Claude Code, or npm to install it." then "./setup.sh" and "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: A newcomer can say in one sentence what firstmate is and who it is for. Defining words like captain, yolo, green and red before they are used helps.
findings.source: What firstmate is: "Firstmate is a tool for people who direct AI coding agents. It keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a worker..."

findings.text: The core track still uses dense script-level detail, such as exit codes, locks, "guarded fast-forward" and "unheld, unblocked". A newcomer who only wants the gist has to read through this before reaching "Why it is built this way".
findings.source: When things go wrong, and what is not limited: "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: Five terms used in the main text are openly left undefined, and so is "in scope". This is honest, but a newcomer is left with gaps right where the page explains how failures and merges work.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." / "does not define a durable record." / "does not define an endpoint." / "does not define a heartbeat." / "does not define a wake."

findings.text: Minor mismatch: four subheadings follow, starting with "Words used first", not three. This can briefly confuse a reader using the page's own map.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: These passages describe Athena's internal process and repository layout rather than what the reader can use. They are clear about the study's limits (nothing was run) but add little for a newcomer.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..." and About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data"
